error_modes.label: Course deviation from the assigned radial

texts.0: SP, due to a correction started only after the CDI had already moved well off centre, did not stop the deviation from the assigned radial. Course error exceeded 8 deg and kept increasing, with the aircraft crossing the course a second time before any adequate heading was flown. IP intervened and directed the heading required to regain the assigned radial.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections sized without regard to the drift already present, did not arrest the deviation from the assigned radial. Course error reached 8 deg and stayed at that value until the IP prompted verbally. SP then regained the course, but the recovery followed the prompt and was not initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to late recognition of the CDI trend, did not begin the correction at the first indication of drift off the assigned radial. Course error reached 7 deg before an adequate intercept heading was applied. SP recognized the deviation and returned inside 5 deg in good time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned radial within 5 deg throughout the intercept and the tracking that followed. Corrections were applied at the first CDI movement and were sized so that the course was regained without overshoot.
texts.4: SP held the assigned radial with the CDI centred, with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg at any point of the intercept. Each correction was anticipated from the rate of needle movement rather than from its displacement, so the course was flown with no visible needle excursion.
texts.marginal: SP kept the course deviation inside the 5 deg standard, but the CDI was repeatedly allowed to reach about 4 deg before a correction was applied. The corrections were triggered by displacement rather than by trend, which left a thin margin to the standard on the outbound leg. SP is expected to correct at the first needle movement so that the deviation stays within 2 to 3 deg.

error_modes.label: Solution of the intercept problem and choice of intercept angle

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete mental model of the intercept sequence that was not updated when the clearance changed, did not solve the problem of the course intercept according to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3. SP turned in the wrong direction for the assigned radial and established a heading that diverged from the course. Deviation opened past 8 deg and IP intervened to set the correct intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an aircraft state that had diverged from the SP's mental model without being reassessed, did not determine the required intercept angle before starting the turn. The angle selected was too small for the displacement and the deviation held at 8 deg with no closure on the course. SP revised the angle only after the IP identified the error verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to retention of the briefed mental model after the assigned radial had been changed, did not compute the intercept from the current position relative to the course. The first intercept heading was in error and the deviation grew to 7 deg. SP reassessed the geometry, selected an adequate angle and regained the course inside 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP solved the intercept problem correctly, determining the direction of turn and the intercept angle from the current position relative to the assigned course, in accordance with the standardized procedures. The selected angle brought the aircraft onto the course without overshoot and without any prompt from the IP.
texts.4: SP solved the intercept problem immediately and without hesitation, matching the intercept angle to both the displacement and the closure rate. The solution was stated before the turn, required no revision on any of the intercepts, and the course was joined with the CDI centred.
texts.marginal: SP solved the intercept problem correctly, but only after a pause during which the aircraft continued away from the assigned course. No deviation exceeded the standard, yet each solution was reached late enough that a larger intercept angle was then needed to recover the displacement. SP is expected to determine the direction of turn and the intercept angle before the displacement grows.

error_modes.label: Lead point and rollout onto the course

texts.0: SP, due to a high intercept angle flown with no lead computed for the closure rate, did not use the appropriate lead when rolling out on the assigned course. SP flew through the course and reached a deviation beyond 8 deg on the opposite side. IP intervened and directed the turn back to the assigned radial.
texts.1: SP, due to a lead taken from the CDI centring instead of from the closure rate, did not start the rollout in time on the assigned course. The overshoot reached 8 deg before any correction began, and the correction started only after the IP called the overshoot. SP then re-intercepted, but the recovery followed the prompt rather than SP's own assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to an underestimated closure rate on a 45 deg intercept, did not apply the appropriate lead when joining the assigned course. The overshoot reached 7 deg on the far side of the course. SP recognized it at once, re-intercepted and settled inside 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP used the appropriate lead for the intercept angle and closure rate flown, beginning the rollout so that the aircraft settled on the assigned course within 5 deg. No overshoot required a second intercept and no prompting was needed.
texts.4: SP judged the lead precisely at every intercept angle flown, rolling out so that the CDI centred as the wings came level. The course was joined without overshoot and without any subsequent correction on any of the intercepts.
texts.marginal: SP used a lead that placed the aircraft on course within the standard, but the rollout consistently ended 3 to 4 deg on the far side before the course settled. The rollout was started late at the higher intercept angles. SP is expected to scale the lead with the closure rate so that the course is joined without crossing it.

error_modes.label: Inbound and outbound tracking and wind correction

texts.0: SP, due to a wind correction angle that was never established after the course was joined, did not execute the inbound and outbound tracking timely and correctly. Drift accumulated on both legs and the deviation passed 8 deg without any heading change. IP intervened and set the heading required to hold the assigned course.
texts.1: SP, due to corrections applied in fixed increments without bracketing the drift, did not track the assigned radial correctly. The deviation stabilized at 8 deg with no wind correction angle established. SP bracketed the drift and regained the course only after verbal direction from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction angle carried over unchanged from the inbound to the outbound leg, did not adjust the heading for the reversed drift after the course reversal. The deviation opened to 6 deg outbound. SP recognized the trend, bracketed the drift and regained the course inside 5 deg on his own.
texts.3: SP executed the inbound and outbound tracking timely and correctly, establishing a wind correction angle that held the deviation within 5 deg on both legs. Corrections were bracketed and reduced in size as the drift was identified.
texts.4: SP established the wind correction angle within the first seconds of each leg and held the assigned course with the CDI centred inbound and outbound. Drift was identified from the rate of needle movement and corrected before any measurable displacement developed.
texts.marginal: SP tracked the course inbound and outbound within the standard, but the wind correction angle was found by repeated symmetric corrections rather than by bracketing, leaving a slow oscillation of about 4 deg either side of the course. Tracking accuracy is met but not consolidated, particularly on the outbound leg. SP is expected to bracket the drift and settle on a single wind correction angle.

error_modes.label: Station passage and immediate outbound re-intercept

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the station, did not identify station passage from the TO/FROM reversal and the CDI behavior. SP chased the reversing needle instead of holding the computed outbound heading, and the course error exceeded 8 deg once the area of unreliable indications was left behind. IP intervened and re-established the outbound course.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness after the change of sequence at the station, did not hold the computed heading through the area of CDI unreliability at station passage. The needle was chased throughout the passage and the deviation stood at 8 deg after the station. SP set the correct outbound heading only after the IP identified station passage verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to situational awareness limited to the instrument in use at the moment of station passage, did not start the outbound intercept immediately after the TO/FROM reversal. The delay allowed the deviation to reach 6 deg on the outbound radial. SP then recognized the passage, applied an adequate intercept angle and regained the course without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP identified station passage from the TO/FROM reversal, held the computed heading through the unreliable indications, then intercepted the outbound radial immediately and tracked it within 5 deg. No prompting was required at any point of the passage.
texts.4: SP anticipated station passage, held the outbound heading through the unreliable CDI indications without a single correction, and re-established the outbound course with the needle centred as soon as the indications settled. The transition from inbound to outbound was continuous, with no measurable deviation.
texts.marginal: SP handled the intercept immediately after station passage within the standard, but reacted to the first CDI fluctuations before the passage was confirmed, and the outbound course was re-established with about 4 deg of deviation. The technique depends on catching the reversal late rather than anticipating it. SP is expected to hold the computed heading through the area of unreliable indications and to start the outbound intercept at the confirmed passage.

error_modes.label: Navaid tuning, identification and course setting for the intercept

texts.0: SP, due to a course set on the OBS that did not match the assigned radial and a navaid that was never identified, did not establish the correct reference before executing the intercept. The aircraft was flown accurately to a course other than the one assigned, leaving an error far beyond 8 deg from the cleared radial. IP intervened and reset the navigation reference.
texts.1: SP, due to an omitted check of the tuned frequency and identifier before starting the intercept, did not confirm that the displayed course was the assigned one. The intercept was flown against an offset course setting and the error remained at 8 deg from the assigned radial. SP corrected the setting only after the IP called for the identification check.
texts.2: SP, due to setting the OBS after the turn had already been started, did not have the intercept reference established before the maneuver. The initial heading was flown against the previous course setting and the deviation reached 6 deg. SP detected the error from the CDI behavior, reset the course and regained the assigned radial without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP tuned, identified and set the navaid for the assigned course before each intercept, so that every intercept was flown against a verified reference. Course settings matched the assignment throughout and no correction of the setup was required.
texts.4: SP completed the tune, identify and set sequence ahead of every intercept and cross-checked the displayed course against the clearance before turning. The navigation reference was correct on every leg, including the change between VOR/TACAN and GPS OBS mode, with no interruption of the tracking.
texts.marginal: SP set and identified the navaid correctly, but the sequence was completed only just before the turn was required, leaving no margin for a setup error. The setup meets the standard while remaining reactive to the clearance rather than anticipating it. SP is expected to complete tune, identify and set early enough to cross-check the course before the intercept begins.

error_modes.label: Basic aircraft control while working the intercept

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the course indication at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not maintain the Basic A/C Control Criteria while flying the intercept. Altitude departed by more than 300 ft and airspeed by more than 20 KIAS during the intercept turn. IP intervened to recover the assigned altitude and airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by the navigation display while the aircraft state went unmonitored, did not hold altitude and heading during the intercept. Altitude reached 300 ft below the assigned level and the rollout heading was 10 deg in error. SP restored both parameters only after the IP called the deviations.
texts.2: SP, due to absorption in the course indication during the intercept turn, did not maintain the Basic A/C Control Criteria at the required standard. Altitude deviated by 250 ft and airspeed by 15 KIAS while the turn was flown. SP resumed the cross-check, corrected both and returned inside 150 ft and 10 KIAS without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft, airspeed within 10 KIAS and heading within 5 deg throughout the intercepts while working the course problem. The instrument cross-check continued through the turns and the navigation task did not displace aircraft control.
texts.4: SP flew the intercepts with altitude, airspeed and heading effectively constant, with deviations not exceeding 50 ft and 5 KIAS. Trim was used so that the aircraft held the parameters while attention was given to the course, and the cross-check remained continuous through every turn.
texts.marginal: SP held the Basic A/C Control Criteria inside the standards, but altitude drifted to about 120 ft during each intercept turn and was recovered only after the turn was completed. The scan narrows towards the navigation display whenever the intercept problem is being solved. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running through the turn so that altitude does not move more than 50 ft.

error_modes.label: INBOUND INTERCEPT ANGLE AT OR BEYOND THE 90 DEG INDEX

texts.0: SP, due to an inbound intercept heading built with the course arrow below the 90 deg index, did not keep the intercept angle less than 90 deg as the technique requires. The aircraft closed the course almost perpendicular to it, the CDI swung across the case faster than the rollout could absorb and the deviation opened beyond 8 deg on the far side. IP intervened and directed the heading required to regain the assigned radial.
texts.1: SP, due to an intercept angle taken up to the 90 deg index for a displacement that did not call for it, did not limit the inbound intercept angle as the technique requires. Closure could not be judged from the needle rate and the overshoot settled at 8 deg on the opposite side of the course. SP reduced the angle and re-intercepted only after the IP called the excessive intercept angle.
texts.2: SP, due to an inbound intercept angle selected close to the 90 deg index for a small displacement, did not keep the course arrow in the upper half of the case as the technique requires. Closure was faster than the lead allowed and the deviation reached 7 deg past the course. SP recognized the geometry, reduced the intercept angle and settled within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP kept every inbound intercept angle less than 90 deg, with the course arrow above the 90 deg index, and sized the angle to the number of degrees off the selected course. Closure stayed controllable and the assigned radial was joined within 5 deg on each intercept.
texts.4: SP selected inbound intercept angles well inside the 90 deg limit and varied them with both the displacement and the rate of intercept desired. The course arrow stayed high in the case on every intercept, closure was uniform and the radial was joined with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP kept the inbound intercept angles below 90 deg, but the course arrow was worked close to the 90 deg index whenever the displacement was large, and the resulting closure left about 4 deg of overshoot before the course settled. The deviation stayed inside the standard, yet the angle is being chosen at the edge of the limit rather than for the rate of intercept desired. SP is expected to keep the course arrow clearly above the 90 deg index so that closure remains controllable at rollout.

error_modes.label: TURN IN THE SHORTER DIRECTION TOWARD THE CDI

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started the longer way round instead of in the shorter direction toward the CDI, did not place the head of the course arrow in the top half of the instrument case. The aircraft turned away from the assigned course through more than 180 deg of heading change and the deviation opened past 8 deg while the turn continued. IP intervened and reversed the turn onto a usable intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a direction of turn taken from the heading difference alone instead of from the position of the CDI, did not turn the shorter way toward the needle. The intercept was set up from the wrong side, the deviation stood at 8 deg and showed no closure on the course. SP reversed the turn only after the IP identified the wrong direction verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a turn begun before the side of the CDI was checked, did not turn in the shorter direction toward the course on the first intercept. The deviation grew to 7 deg during the reversal of the turn. SP identified the error when the head of the course arrow left the top half of the case, reversed the turn and regained the course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP turned in the shorter direction toward the CDI on every intercept, placing the head of the course arrow in the top half of the instrument case before rolling out on the intercept heading. The direction of turn was correct throughout and the assigned course was joined within 5 deg.
texts.4: SP established the direction of turn from the side of the CDI immediately on each clearance, with no hesitation and no reversal at any point. The head of the course arrow was in the top half of the case from the start of every turn and the course was joined with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP turned the shorter way toward the CDI on each intercept, but the direction was confirmed after the bank was already established rather than before it, and one intercept was flown out to about 4 deg while the geometry was checked. Deviations stayed inside the standard while the direction of turn is still being verified late. SP is expected to read the side of the CDI and place the head of the course arrow in the top half of the case before starting the turn.

error_modes.label: TO INDICATION CHECK AFTER SETTING THE INBOUND COURSE

texts.0: SP, due to an omitted check for a TO indication after setting the inbound course, did not confirm that the radial had been converted into an inbound course before starting the intercept. The reciprocal was left in the course window, corrections were flown in the direction opposite to the needle and the deviation ran beyond 8 deg. IP intervened, reset the inbound course and directed the intercept.
texts.1: SP, due to a course set from the radial without checking the TO or FROM indication, did not verify the course reference before the intercept. The CDI was displaced with a FROM indication on an inbound leg, the corrections did not close the course and the deviation held at 8 deg. SP reset the inbound course only after the IP called for the TO check.
texts.2: SP, due to the TO indication being read only after the intercept turn had begun, did not check the course window before starting the intercept. The first correction was applied against a reversed sense and the deviation reached 7 deg. SP caught the FROM indication, reset the inbound course and regained the radial within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP set the inbound course, converting the assigned radial where required, and checked for a TO indication before every intercept. Sensing was correct throughout, corrections closed the course and the deviation stayed within 5 deg.
texts.4: SP converted each assigned radial to the inbound course and confirmed the TO indication as part of the setup, before any turn was started. Sensing was verified on every intercept without prompting and the course was flown with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP checked the TO indication on each inbound course, but the check was made only as the turn was rolling in, and on one intercept the sense was confirmed with the CDI already about 4 deg out. The deviations remained inside the standard while verification is still being done after the turn is committed. SP is expected to check for the TO indication immediately after setting the inbound course and before the intercept turn.

error_modes.label: CONSTRUCTION OF THE INBOUND INTERCEPT HEADING FROM THE BEARING POINTER

texts.0: SP, due to an inbound intercept heading that was estimated instead of being built from the course arrow to the bearing pointer and 30 deg beyond it, did not determine a heading that would close the assigned course. The heading flown fell short of the bearing pointer, the aircraft paralleled the radial and the deviation stayed beyond 8 deg with no closure. IP intervened and set the correct intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an intercept heading taken to the bearing pointer without continuing 30 deg past it, did not establish an angle that would bring the aircraft onto the assigned course. Closure was negligible and the deviation remained at the 8 deg limit for the whole leg. SP added the required intercept angle only after the IP prompted with the heading to fly.
texts.2: SP, due to the 30 deg increment being applied from the course arrow instead of from the bearing pointer, did not build the inbound intercept heading as the technique describes. The resulting angle was too small for the displacement and the deviation reached 7 deg before closure began. SP rebuilt the heading from the bearing pointer and joined the course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP built each inbound intercept heading from the course arrow, up the case to the bearing pointer and 30 deg beyond it, and flew that heading until the rollout. The angle produced steady closure and the assigned course was joined within 5 deg on every intercept.
texts.4: SP produced the inbound intercept heading immediately on each clearance, moving from the course arrow to the bearing pointer and adding the intercept increment without hesitation. Closure was uniform, no heading required revision and the course was joined with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP built the inbound intercept headings from the bearing pointer correctly, but the increment was worked out only after the turn had started and one heading was refined in flight, leaving the deviation at about 4 deg when closure finally began. Accuracy is inside the standard while the heading is being produced late. SP is expected to read the course arrow, the bearing pointer and the intercept increment as one step before the turn.

error_modes.label: OUTBOUND INTERCEPT HEADING AND THE 45 DEG INTERCEPT ANGLE

texts.0: SP, due to an outbound intercept heading that was not built from the tail of the bearing pointer to the course arrow and 45 deg beyond it, did not establish an angle capable of intercepting the outbound course. The heading flown diverged from the desired outbound course and the deviation ran beyond 8 deg and continued to grow. IP intervened and set the outbound intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to an outbound intercept angle reduced well below the 45 deg the technique recommends, did not obtain a usable rate of intercept on the outbound course. The CDI moved so slowly that the deviation held at 8 deg for the whole leg. SP increased the intercept angle only after the IP directed the heading to fly.
texts.2: SP, due to the 45 deg increment being applied from the tail of the bearing pointer instead of from the course arrow, did not build the outbound intercept heading as the technique describes. The angle was in error and the deviation reached 7 deg before the course began to close. SP rebuilt the heading from the course arrow and joined the outbound course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP built each outbound intercept heading from the tail of the bearing pointer, up the case to the course arrow and 45 deg beyond it, having first set the desired outbound course. The rate of intercept was suitable and the outbound course was joined within 5 deg.
texts.4: SP set the desired outbound course and produced the intercept heading with the standard 45 deg angle without hesitation, adjusting it only where the rate of intercept desired called for it. Every outbound course was joined smoothly with deviations not exceeding 1 to 2 deg.
texts.marginal: SP used the standard 45 deg outbound intercept angle and joined the course inside the standard, but the angle was applied without regard to the displacement, so the small intercepts were flown at an unnecessarily high rate and closed with about 4 deg of overshoot. The result meets the standard while the angle is being used as a fixed value. SP is expected to start from 45 deg and adjust it to the rate of intercept desired.

error_modes.label: DRIFT CORRECTION COMPUTED FROM CROSSWIND AND TRUE AIRSPEED

texts.0: SP, due to a drift correction that was never computed from the crosswind component and the true airspeed in NM per minute, did not correct for winds while maintaining the assigned course. The heading was held equal to the course, drift was allowed to run unopposed and the deviation passed 8 deg and continued to open. IP intervened and set the heading required to hold the course.
texts.1: SP, due to a drift correction guessed instead of derived from the crosswind component divided by the true airspeed in NM per minute, did not apply a correction that matched the wind. The correction was several degrees short of the drift and the deviation stabilized at the 8 deg limit. SP recomputed and applied an adequate correction only after the IP called the drift.
texts.2: SP, due to a crosswind component estimated from the forecast rather than from the wind actually observed, did not compute a drift correction adequate for the leg. The correction was undersized and the deviation reached 7 deg before it was noticed. SP recomputed the correction from the crosswind and the airspeed in NM per minute and regained the course inside 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP computed the drift correction by dividing the crosswind component by the true airspeed in NM per minute and applied it as soon as the course was joined. The wind correction angle held the deviation within 5 deg on both the inbound and the outbound legs.
texts.4: SP computed the drift correction from the crosswind component and the true airspeed before joining the course and applied it at rollout, so that the CDI stayed centred from the start of the leg. The correction was refined by no more than 1 to 2 deg and the course was held with no visible needle movement.
texts.marginal: SP computed a drift correction from the crosswind component and the airspeed, but rounded it down and held the reduced value, so the course was maintained with a slow drift that reached about 4 deg before each additional correction. Accuracy stays inside the standard while the computed correction is not being applied in full. SP is expected to apply the correction obtained from the crosswind divided by the true airspeed in NM per minute and to refine it from the observed drift.

error_modes.label: MARKING THE INTERCEPT HEADING WITH THE HEADING BUG

texts.0: SP, due to an intercept heading that was never marked with the heading bug and was then lost while the navigation display was being worked, did not fly the heading computed for the intercept. The rollout was made on a heading far from the one required, the course was not closed and the deviation exceeded 8 deg. IP intervened and directed the intercept heading.
texts.1: SP, due to the heading bug being left where the previous leg had set it, did not have the computed intercept heading marked during the turn. The rollout was 10 deg off the required heading and the deviation remained at the 8 deg limit until the IP called the heading error. SP then flew the computed heading, but only after the prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to the heading bug being set only after the turn had been started, did not have the intercept heading marked at the moment of rollout. The rollout was about 8 deg off the computed heading and the deviation reached 7 deg before the error was seen. SP set the bug, corrected onto the computed heading and joined the course within 5 deg without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP marked the computed intercept heading with the heading bug before each turn and rolled out within 5 deg of it. The bug was reset for the next leg as the course was joined and no intercept heading had to be recalled from memory.
texts.4: SP set the heading bug on the computed intercept heading as part of the solution and rolled out on it within 2 deg on every intercept. The bug was moved to the wind corrected heading once the course was joined, so the reference on the case always matched the heading being flown.
texts.marginal: SP marked the intercept headings with the heading bug and held them inside the standard, but the bug was set as the bank was going in rather than before the turn, and one rollout finished about 4 deg off the computed heading. Performance meets the standard while the reference is still being set under time pressure. SP is expected to mark the intercept heading with the bug as soon as it is computed and before the turn is started.
